dialogue.title: Fort Solid at night
paragraphs: The fort's curfew escorts you away; it does not order Soldiers or Captain Eir to attack you. See Eir's nighttime rules for the hours, perimeter and story permissions. Attacking friendly characters can still cause retaliation; see Aggression rules.

dialogue.title: Information
paragraphs: Eir explains that newcomers may visit Magus Clay in the undercroft during the day, but must leave the fort's perimeter at night. Clay buys and sells supplies there. Her Information option disappears once she grants access to the commander.

dialogue.title: Advice
paragraphs: Early on, Eir suggests visiting the two other Unwanted at the camp marked on your starting map. This is the lead into the camp investigation, not a repeatable errand.
After you hand over the Wooden Recorder, choosing Advice goes straight to her survival tips instead. Before that, More Advice follows the camp suggestion.

dialogue.title: More Advice
paragraphs: Eir recommends preparing above ground before exploring caves: collect larger branches from dead trees during daylight, look for Flint among rocks, and build a Campfire before a cold night.

This is preparation advice, not a cave-entry requirement. Tree harvesting and Ground debris explain the material sources. A campfire needs fuel and a separate ignition attempt; Temperature explains warmth, wet clothing and exposure.

dialogue.title: Fort Solid at night
paragraphs: The curfew causes an escort-out scene, not a night-only attack by Soldiers or Eir. It checks after a turn advances the clock, from 21:00 through 05:00 inclusive. At exactly 05:00 it still applies; after 05:00 and before 21:00 it does not. These are fixed hours, not the lighting system's dusk or dawn.

Until you earn permission to remain, the outdoor check covers a 10-tile radius around the fort's reference point, not its entire world-map zone. Inside Clay's undercroft, the early-game check applies throughout that interior. A fade moves you out rather than starting a guard fight; the outdoor escort also advances another turn.

The escort check does not require a nearby Soldier or Eir, and is skipped while a screen transition is already running. Their normal friendly targeting and retaliation rules are separate; see Aggression rules.

dialogue.title: Earning nighttime access
paragraphs: The undercroft exemption begins when you deliver the three rift samples to Clay. You may then remain inside at night, although the outdoor perimeter restriction still applies. Continue his conversation for permission to use his storage chest and alchemy station.

The remaining curfew ends after you bring Viend back and speak with Eir. Her invitation to meet Commander Tain grants fort access and removes the outdoor escort restriction. Simply delivering the Wooden Recorder or reaching the next midnight does not lift it.

dialogue.title: Quest guidance
paragraphs: The camp lead continues by taking the Wooden Recorder to Eir. Wait for the next midnight, then speak with her again to be sent to Clay. Returning immediately at midnight can still trigger the curfew; the quest timer and nighttime access are different rules.
Once Clay has the rift samples, Eir supplies the direction to Ranger Bhato. Follow the journal's direction for your world and Bhato's location instructions.

dialogue.title: Clay's whereabouts
paragraphs: After you report Scaal's defeat, Eir has a Clay? topic. She has heard that magi keep hidden realms opened with a magical key, and suggests finding someone who sells magical items: Grand Mother sells Magus' Shard.
Once Clay is dead, talking to Eir closes his story and the journal.

dialogue.title: Advice
paragraphs: Clay recommends searching beneath rocks and boulders for useful finds, including small animals, and examining creatures before fighting them.

Ground debris and Searching boulders list the possible finds and their conditions; a search does not guarantee every item he mentions. Use Examine to inspect a creature rather than guessing its capabilities. The Bestiary, Health and armor and Damage types pages explain the combat information.

dialogue.title: Undercroft at night
paragraphs: Early visits to the undercroft are subject to Eir's nighttime rules. The undercroft earns its own exemption before the rest of the fort; see nighttime access for the quest requirements.

dialogue.title: Quest guidance
paragraphs: After Eir sends you to him, Clay requests three rift samples. Handing them over advances his research; continue talking to obtain access to the storage chest and Alchemy workstation, then return to Eir.

Later, bring Bhato's rune to Clay. He provides Clay's Strange Potion for the return to the dead camp. His subsequent instructions send you to investigate ruins and warn about the toadkin around them. Follow the journal's old-records objective rather than treating his ordinary Advice option as another quest.

dialogue.title: Later story

dialogue.title: Quest guidance
paragraphs: When Eir sends you to Bhato, he describes a poisonous Sceetler that fled into an ancient cellar and gives you two Minor Antidotes. Follow the cellar objective, not the entrance to his hut. Poison explains the damage and remedies.
Recover the creature's rune and report back to Bhato. His reward conversation unlocks his storage chest and Workstation and sends you to Clay with the rune.
Bhato's hideout is in a Common Bog directly north, south, east or west of Fort Solid, never diagonally. Its zone is chosen at world creation.

Neighboring zones are checked north, south, east for a column A fort, or west, north, south for a column E fort. At most one becomes Vast Waters; the rest become Common Bogs. Bhato takes the last Common Bog in that order, so directions are not equally likely.
Captain Eir gives the direction, which is recorded in your journal. Look for a small foliage-roof hut, placed when you first enter its zone. Enter the hut, not the nearby ancient cellar.

dialogue.title: Information
paragraphs: Viend says he formerly practiced healing magic and was exiled for helping people the Kingdom rejected. Continue the conversation to hear why he dislikes the magi's practice of treating everyone else as inferior.
These two Information responses describe his background; they are not a request to collect items. His later trading access is separate from this conversation.

dialogue.title: Quest guidance
paragraphs: After his revival, Viend asks you to escort him to Fort Solid because Eir still believes him dead. Follow Escort Viend and then A successful return. Talking to Eir afterward is also the step that earns full nighttime access.

ability.title: Healing
paragraphs: Viend automatically heals up to two ordinary wounds on one character within 16 tiles. Each cast restores 1 HP to each of two randomly chosen wounded health cells, or just 1 HP if only one cell is wounded. It costs him 10 action points, his full turn's allowance, and has no separate cooldown.

The player always takes priority, even if someone else is closer or more badly injured. Otherwise, Viend heals himself if wounded, then the nearest eligible friendly character. He does not heal dead or incapacitated NPCs. Walls and other obstacles do not block the spell. He does not heal Wilda, Grand Mother or the Survivors.

Healing restores HP, not armor or wellbeing, and does not remove poison, bleeding or sickness. Burns cannot be healed directly: use Simple Burn Remedy to turn them into ordinary wounds first. See Resting for natural wound healing.

Viend checks for wounds before moving or attacking whenever he can act with all 10 action points available. Ongoing damage or a stun can delay or prevent his action. Healing needs no conversation, payment or supplies, works outside combat, and does not depend on his shop or alchemy workstation.

During his escort or an active summon, Viend receives an action each turn. When nearby but idle, neither fighting nor detecting an enemy, he normally has a 10% chance to act each turn, so healing can be intermittent. While you rest in a bed or sleeping gear, this idle chance falls to 1.5% if at least two conditions are met: satiation above its low threshold, stamina above its low threshold, and temperature inside its comfortable range.

Gurb-Gurb's hollow is placed when you first enter a Drowned Fen while it remains uncreated. Revisits and loading an outdoor save also trigger the check; caves do not. A Savage Mirk is eligible only in a world with no Drowned Fen. Normal new worlds always have one.

dialogue.title: Information
paragraphs: Ihar says he fled to the Mirk while still wanted by the Kingdom, rather than being sentenced to exile as an Unwanted. Continue to hear about his failed rebellion and his doubts about his own ambitions.
This is character history, not a rebellion quest or a requirement for buying his goods.

dialogue.title: Trade
paragraphs: Ihar explains that he claimed the shipwreck and its cargo of military equipment after losing his own boat. This supplies the background to his shop, not a separate treasure-recovery objective. His wares are listed below.

Ihar lives in a wooden shipwreck on a Broken Fen shoreline. Entering a Broken Fen attempts to place it if it has not appeared yet. A search can fail after 1280 attempts to find suitable sand and water, even when a valid spot exists.

After a failed search, enter the same or another Broken Fen to retry. Revisits and loading an outdoor save count; caves do not. There is no fallback to another area type. Normal new worlds have Broken Fens; a world without them cannot place this wreck.
Once placed, the wreck stays in that location. Ihar is inside.

classifications.summary: Wilda leads the Survivors' camp. She trades supplies, gives the camp's request to hunt The Terror, and can later be summoned as an ally.

paragraphs: Wilda leads the Survivors' camp, which is built the first time you enter a Savage Mirk area in a world. A message about torchlight and five white dots point toward it when it appears. There is only one camp per world.

The camp has three huts, two permanent torches and a cleared yard. Wilda and three Survivor guards stay nearby. Grand Mother lives inside the main hut, whose ladder stays locked until Wilda trusts you.
You may not place or build anything within about 26 tiles of the camp. Mirkfangs and other creatures do not spawn within 16 tiles of it. The Terror gives up a chase when you step inside that range.

dialogue.title: First meeting
paragraphs: Wilda first checks that you are not working for the Kingdom, then lets you visit the camp. She forbids building nearby and keeps Grand Mother off-limits until you earn her trust. Trade opens after this introduction.

dialogue.title: Information
paragraphs: Wilda and Grand Mother are exiles who have survived in the Mirk for months. They gathered other exiles, who now call themselves Survivors, and settled in the Savage Mirk because Fort Solid would not tolerate a growing group nearby. Grand Mother's calming presence holds them together.

dialogue.title: Trust
paragraphs: Choosing Trust starts the camp's request: kill The Terror and bring Wilda the Head of The Terror. The Terror is a Mirkfang Matriarch that only hunts the camp's area at night, never close to the camp, and only after Wilda has asked.
Talk to Wilda while carrying the head. She keeps it, unlocks the ladder to Grand Mother's hut and adds herself to the Summoning Stone's list of allies.

classifications.note: Renamed from Unwanted Guard in 0.9.0.0 and moved to the camp faction. NPC grouping follows its friendly faction and camp role.
classifications.summary: Survivors guard the Survivors' camp. They do not hold conversations: talking to one gets a short greeting, friendlier once Wilda trusts you. They warn you off if you try to build near the camp. A Survivor's corpse holds random treasure.

paragraphs: Three Survivors guard the Survivors' camp with Wilda. They stay near the camp rather than roaming the Savage Mirk.

classifications.summary: Grand Mother is Wilda's grandmother. She has no attack. Her blessing grants a skill point, and she sells the game's magic weapons.

paragraphs: Grand Mother sits inside the main hut of the Survivors' camp. Its ladder is locked until Wilda trusts you; see Wilda's Trust topic.

dialogue.title: Blessing
paragraphs: Grand Mother greets each newcomer with a blessing. Finishing this first conversation grants one skill point. Trade, Information and Advice become available afterward.

dialogue.title: Information
paragraphs: Grand Mother is Wilda's grandmother and was also the wise woman of their home village. She describes such wise women as gifted in ways similar to magi, which the Kingdom does not tolerate.

dialogue.title: Advice

dialogue.title: Trade

classifications.summary: The Terror is the boss of the Survivors' camp request: an unusually tough Mirkfang Matriarch with armored body cells. She can attack twice in a turn when she does not move, and her bites deal Leeching damage.

ability.title: Where to find her
paragraphs: Wilda describes her this way: "She stalks this area at night... She is a clever one, she never goes near our camp."

The Terror does not exist until you choose Trust in Wilda's conversation. After that she can appear only at night, only outdoors, and only in the Savage Mirk area that holds the Survivors' camp. She never appears in any other area. Only one exists at a time, and none appear again once she is dead.

She is never placed within 16 tiles (256 px) of the camp's main hut. Anywhere else in that area is possible. An area is 160 x 160 tiles, so she can be anywhere from 16 tiles to roughly 105-170 tiles from the camp, depending on where the camp sits. She is never placed on water or sand, within about 5 tiles of the area's edge, or on screen.

Each night turn, a new creature may appear somewhere off screen in that area. When one does, it is The Terror about 1 time in 6. Creatures off screen do not move, so she waits where she appeared until you come close. Dawn does not remove her, but while she is off screen and not hunting you, she has a 2% chance each turn to vanish. A new one can then appear on a later night.

To find her, walk the area at night away from the camp, ideally beyond 16 tiles. Every third turn while she has a target, The Terror screeches instead of attacking. The screech removes 25% focus directly; difficulty and Focused Mind do not reduce it.

If she is chasing you and you step within 16 tiles of the camp, she screeches and gives up the chase. If she is already next to you, she can still bite. Her corpse always holds the Head of The Terror, plus bat meat and hides.

classifications.note: Boss form of Magus Clay, grouped as an enemy because it always attacks; the friendly NPC record is separate.
classifications.summary: Clay's boss form waits in his hidden Magus realm, reached with Magus' Shard after you report Scaal's defeat to Eir. He fights with fire spells at range and in melee. Defeating him continues the main quest.

ability.title: Blink and rewards
paragraphs: This is the same Magus Clay who trades and gives advice in Fort Solid's undercroft earlier in the story. Throw Magus' Shard to open the portal to his realm.
Clay starts the fight as soon as you arrive. Every third turn while he has a target, he teleports to a random free spot in the realm at least 7 tiles from you, usually 10 or more.
His corpse holds 6 to 10 Gold Coins, Clay's Magus Hood and Magi's Ropebelt.
Each of his 49 hit points has one layer of armor, which must be broken before that cell can be damaged.

entry_display.summary: Take the Wooden Recorder recovered from Dead Unwanted at the dead camp to Captain Eir. Speaking to Eir while carrying it automatically hands over one recorder and advances the investigation; this is not a sale.
Eir has received the recorder. Wait until the next midnight before returning to her.
After the midnight rollover, speak with Captain Eir again to continue the investigation.

entry_display.title: Effects
entry_display.summary: Move through vegetation and obstacles more efficiently: each rank adds 8% traversal efficiency. Every third rank also improves your ability to form paths.

entry_display.title: Effects
entry_display.summary: Travel through water more efficiently, gaining 8% efficiency per rank. At rank 10, swimming drains half as much stamina.

entry_display.title: Effects
entry_display.summary: Jumper increases the maximum jump range and lowers the AP cost of jumping. A jump costs 8 AP multiplied by its distance divided by the maximum range, rounded to the nearest 0.2 AP, so a jump at full range costs 8 AP at any rank. Distance is measured in a straight line between tile centers: a diagonal neighbor is about 1.41 tiles away.
notes: Water: jumping out of medium-depth water adds 3 AP to the 8 AP base, and deep water adds 7 AP. Jumping is impossible from the deepest water.
Higher ground: jumping up onto a higher terrain level adds 8 AP to the base. Standing on raised footing, such as an obstacle, reduces either penalty by 3 AP, or by 6 AP on higher footing.
Encumbrance: the cost is multiplied by 1.2 when overburdened, 1.6 when very overburdened (10 or more over the carry limit) and 2.0 when extremely overburdened (20 or more over).
A target beyond the maximum range is pulled back toward the jumper. A jump that costs more than the maximum AP cannot be made.
entry_display.example: For example, a jump to an adjacent tile on flat, dry ground costs 8 x 1 / 2 = 4.0 AP at rank 0. At rank 10 the range is 4.75 tiles, so the same jump costs 8 x 1 / 4.75 = 1.68, shown in game as 1.6 AP. The screenshots below show the cost of an adjacent jump and a two-tile jump at each rank.

entry_display.title: Effects
entry_display.summary: Climb slopes more efficiently, with a 6% improvement per rank.

entry_display.title: Effects
entry_display.summary: Keep your footing when you might slip or be knocked off balance. Each rank gives an 8% chance to avoid the loss of balance.

entry_display.title: Effects
entry_display.summary: Start fires more reliably. Each rank adds 3 percentage points to the success chance of a fire-starting attempt. From rank 5, each turn spent resting or sleeping has a 4% chance to treat one burnt hit point, turning it into an ordinary wound; from rank 10 the chance is 8%.

entry_display.title: Effects

rules.text: One silver coin has the value of 100 copper coins. One gold coin has the value of 10 silver coins, or 1,000 copper coins.
Offer coins without buying anything, then confirm the trade. The merchant returns change in gold first, then silver, then copper.
rules.qualification: Describe descending-denomination change, not an absolute guarantee of the mathematically fewest coins at every floating-point rounding boundary. Copper change is rounded to a whole coin.

rules.text: The item's base weight is multiplied by its stack quantity. Coin weights are 25 g for copper, 30 g for silver, and 55 g for gold. Consolidating equal value into higher denominations substantially reduces carried weight.
rules.qualification: Use the coin pages as the sole editable home of the individual weights. Kilograms are corroborated by the carry-limit calculation and Pack Mule's localized kilogram-per-rank description. Ordinary coin stacks do not enter the food, special-container or equipped-armor weight adjustments.

rules.text: Shops share the same rates, with no merchant, player or difficulty markup. Purchases use full item value; resale depends on condition. Bought items have full durability and fuel. Quest items cannot be sold. Rift Weave cannot be sold until after Clay's initial sample investigation.
rules.qualification: An unchanged, full-condition item therefore has the same underlying buy and sell value. The affordability check and copper change involve rounding, so do not promise exact conservation of arbitrary sub-copper fractions.

rules.text: Listed wares do not run out, and merchants have unlimited buying funds.
rules.qualification: These rules apply to available shops, not story gifts or exchanges. Dialogue and sale restrictions still apply. Display quantities are samples, not finite stock. Summoned characters cannot be interacted with. Clay, Bhato, Tain, Viend, Gurb-Gurb, Ihar, Wilda and Grand Mother have wares.

rules.text: Resale value is standard value multiplied by remaining durability as a fraction of maximum, with a 10% floor. Half durability gives half value; one-tenth durability or less gives 10%.
rules.qualification: Items without durability use full value. There is no second wear discount.

rules.text: For items with a burn duration and remaining fuel, the fuel fraction replaces the durability factor, with a 25% floor. The two discounts do not multiply.
rules.qualification: Both a burn duration and remaining fuel are required; proximity to fire is not enough.

rules.text: Affordability compares basket totals rounded to whole copper. Change is selling value minus purchase cost: whole gold first, then whole silver, then rounded copper.
rules.qualification: There is no merchant commission. Fractions of a copper can be lost or gained through rounding.

guides.title: Sharp
paragraphs: Sharp attacks add bleeding to unarmored hit points instead of removing them immediately. Bleeding stacks and takes effect at the start of the target's turn.
Remaining bleeding spreads to the next neighboring hit point in a fixed direction. Rotating the attack changes that direction. Spreading bleeding can reach beneath armor.
An initial sharp hit normally removes armor without causing bleeding on that cell. At rank 10, Blade Master lets remaining damage cause bleeding after breaking armor.
Apply an Improvised Bandage or Bandage to bleeding cells. Bandages stop bleeding but do not restore lost hit points.
A bleeding creature keeps taking its turns while it is out of sight or idle, so bleeding keeps working until it stops.

guides.title: Poison
paragraphs: Poison stacks on individual hit points. At the start of the target's turn, a poisoned cell is lost and one poison counter is spent. Remaining poison can spread to a random adjacent healthy cell, including diagonals.
Spreading poison can reach beneath armor. An ordinary direct poison hit removes one armor layer instead of poisoning an armored cell. Thrown poison has different rules; see the flask's effect.
Minor Antidote and Antidote clear poison from the cells they cover without restoring lost hit points. Natural Antidote can reduce poison before it takes effect.
A poisoned creature keeps taking its turns while it is out of sight or idle, so poison keeps working until it runs out.

guides.title: Blunt
paragraphs: Blunt damage removes armor before the protected hit point. A successful blunt attack has a base 10% chance to stun a surviving target, making it lose its next turn.
Master Basher raises stun chance with blunt melee weapons and reduces their AP costs at rank milestones. Blunt orbs get only the base chance.

guides.title: Piercing
paragraphs: Piercing damage removes armor before the protected hit point. After each point of damage, if armor or HP remains on that cell, there is a 15% chance to remove one more layer or hit point.
Multi-point hits can make several checks. Piercing does not bypass armor.

guides.title: Force
paragraphs: Force damage removes armor before the protected hit point. Each positive-damage attack cell that hits a living part of the target has a base 15% chance to deal one extra damage to an eligible neighboring cell.
The extra hit can strike diagonally and must remove armor before HP. Force Fighter raises this chance for force melee weapons only and reduces their AP costs at rank milestones.

guides.title: Fire
paragraphs: Ordinary direct fire attacks remove armor before burning the hit point underneath. Thrown fire has different rules; see the flask's effect. Wound salves and ordinary resting cannot restore burned cells, but Fire Bond from rank 5 and Staff of The Fire Eater can treat them.
Simple Burn Remedy turns a burn into an ordinary wound. It does not restore HP immediately; heal the wound afterward.

guides.title: Weak
paragraphs: Weak damage removes armor before the protected hit point. It has no extra effect: no bleeding, poison, burns, stun, piercing or force damage.

guides.title: Health and armor
paragraphs: Each occupied health-grid cell contains one HP. Empty positions cannot be hit.
Each HP cell can have up to three armor layers. Armor is not extra health.
Place an attack pattern over the target's health grid. Only overlapping cells can hit. Each number is that cell's damage range; rotation and dodging change the overlap.
The grids show starting health and armor. Wounds, story events, equipment, skills, ammunition and status effects can change combat results.
Ammunition adds bonus damage to a bow's pattern. Roll its bonus range separately for each occupied attack cell.
Wellbeing is separate from combat HP. Resting can heal ordinary wounds when its recovery conditions are met, but not burns unless you have Fire Bond at rank 5 or higher.

guides.title: Satiation
paragraphs: Eating restores satiation. On Medium difficulty, an ordinary turn removes 0.715 percentage points before skill modifiers. Resting and sleeping reduce this loss; see Resting.
At 50% or more, satiation adds 0.5 percentage points of wellbeing per turn. From 20% to below 50% it is neutral. Below 20%, the penalty grows to 1 percentage point per turn at zero satiation.
Slow Metabolism reduces satiation loss. Skill and difficulty modifiers multiply; see Wellbeing for difficulty rates.

Eating without getting sick grants Well fed if satiation ends above 90%. Duration depends on the food's base satiation, up to 35 turns. Well fed reduces stamina loss, not wellbeing loss directly; see Stamina.
See Foods for filling meals and sickness risks. Herbivore improves satiation from foods the game treats as plant-based. Casting an essence orb drains satiation; see Magic weapons.
guides.image_caption: Loaf of Bread is one source of satiation.

guides.title: Stamina
paragraphs: Ending a turn restores 4 percentage points of stamina per unused AP, except while swimming or drowning. Spending all AP leaves no ordinary recovery.
At 50% or more, stamina adds 0.2 percentage points of wellbeing per turn. From 20% to below 50% it is neutral. Below 20%, the penalty grows to 0.5 percentage points per turn at zero stamina.

Stamina below 30%, 15% and 5% adds 1, 2 and 3 percentage points of accident risk, respectively: cumulative totals of 1%, 3% and 6%. This applies to actions with accident checks, not every turn. Focus and encumbrance can add more risk.
Well fed halves stamina loss. It multiplies with the difficulty rates on Wellbeing and does not reduce unused-AP recovery. See Satiation for how to gain it.

Swimming drains stamina at turn end instead of restoring it; running out can cause drowning. Beds and bedrolls have their own recovery. Normal AP replenishment pauses in bed, so do not count unused-AP recovery twice. See Resting.
Wayfarer's Vigor restores stamina over time. Bramble Berries and Bursthopper restore it immediately. Casting a wind or storm orb drains stamina; see Magic weapons.
guides.image_caption: Wayfarer's Vigor grants temporary stamina recovery.

guides.title: Focus
paragraphs: On Medium difficulty, an ordinary active turn removes 0.56 percentage points of focus before skill modifiers. Resting and sleeping restore focus and reduce its loss.
At 50% or more, focus adds 0.2 percentage points of wellbeing per turn. From 20% to below 50% it is neutral. Below 20%, the penalty grows to 0.5 percentage points per turn at zero focus.

Focus below 30%, 15% and 5% adds 1, 2 and 3 percentage points of accident risk, respectively: cumulative totals of 1%, 3% and 6%. The action must have an accident check. Stamina and encumbrance can add more risk.

Focused Mind and difficulty modify focus loss, not direct gains from rest or sleep. See Wellbeing for difficulty rates. Casting a poison orb drains focus directly, and The Terror's screech removes 25% at once; neither is reduced by skills or difficulty.

Cranberries restore focus immediately. Magi's Ropebelt restores 4% for every 4 unspent AP when you end a turn standing. Sleep until rested ends at full focus; sleep until sunrise follows the sunrise schedule, not a fixed turn count.
guides.image_caption: A Tattered Bedroll provides a place to rest or sleep.

guides.title: Temperature
paragraphs: The comfortable temperature range is 40-60%. These are game-meter percentages, not degrees. There is no temperature penalty to wellbeing within that range.
Outside the comfortable range, the wellbeing penalty grows to 3 percentage points per turn at either 0% or 100% temperature. High temperature gives no bonus.

Each turn, body temperature moves one third of the way toward local ambient temperature before cooling modifiers. Insulation pulls it toward the comfortable midpoint. Wetness pulls it toward 10%, so rain and immersion can chill you even in mild air.
Body Warmth reduces cooling loss and improves drying. Difficulty also modifies cooling losses, not every temperature change; see Wellbeing.

Nearby active fires warm and dry you. Warm to the core halves ambient cooling; see Wellbeing for its other bonus. Shelter reduces rain exposure and can cool hot conditions. Equipment condition affects insulation and waterproofing; sleeping gear helps while in use.
Pleasant Vegetable Soup, Tasty Crab Soup and Survivor's Delight grant temporary warmth. Baby Firelouse does too, but also causes a fire hit. Casting a fire orb drains warmth; see Magic weapons.
guides.image_caption: An active nearby Campfire can warm and dry you.

guides.title: Wellbeing
paragraphs: Wellbeing is separate from combat HP. Each turn combines Satiation, Stamina, Focus and Temperature with active effects. At zero wellbeing, you die.

A percentage point changes a 0-100% meter; it is not a multiplier. Each meter's wellbeing contribution rounds to 0.1 percentage-point steps before the display settles. All meters stay between zero and 100%.
Warm to the core and Well rested each add 1 percentage point per turn. Well fed instead conserves stamina. See Temperature, Resting and Satiation for their triggers.

Sickness I, II and III remove 1, 2 and 3 percentage points per turn; only the highest active level counts. Being very overburdened removes 1 and extremely overburdened removes 2. The lighter overburdened state increases movement costs and accident risk without a direct wellbeing penalty.

Compared with Medium, Easy multiplies satiation, stamina, focus and cooling losses by 0.67; Hard multiplies them by 1.2. Skill and temporary-effect modifiers multiply with these rates. Direct recovery gains are unaffected, and cooling modifiers do not slow every temperature change.

High wellbeing does not instantly restore combat HP. See Resting for natural wound healing; burns cannot heal this way. If a magic orb costs more of a meter than you have, the shortfall is taken from wellbeing.
Honey improves wellbeing and shortens sickness. Riftvine Berries reduce wellbeing.
guides.image_caption: Honey has a direct wellbeing benefit as well as food value.

guides.title: Resting
paragraphs: Resting and sleeping restore focus and stamina, but time, weather and temperature keep advancing. See Action points for turn duration.
Ground rest adds 2 percentage points of focus per turn and halves ordinary satiation and focus losses. Unused AP restores stamina. Rest ends at full focus and stamina, or when interrupted manually.

Bed and bedroll rest gives the same focus gain and half-rate losses, plus 32 percentage points of stamina per turn. Sleep gives 2.5 focus and 32 stamina, with satiation and focus losses at 35% of normal. Normal AP replenishment pauses in bed; do not double-count stamina recovery.
Sleep until rested ends at full focus; sleep until sunrise follows the sunrise schedule. Disturbance can wake you. Below 45% wellbeing, a falling wellbeing trend can also force you awake.

Sleeping can grant Well rested above 95% focus, with satiation and stamina above 20% and temperature strictly inside its comfortable range. Sleeping-item comfort sets the duration added, up to 35 turns. The timer can pause in bed when at least two of the three supporting conditions hold. See Wellbeing for its bonus.

At 50% wellbeing or more, resting can heal one ordinary wounded combat cell. The chance depends on satiation, stamina, focus and the temperature penalty. With full supporting meters and no temperature penalty, it is 5% per resting turn. Burns cannot heal this way; Fire Bond from rank 5 gives a separate chance to treat one.

Find shelter, warmth and food before a long rest. Sleeping gear contributes insulation and waterproofing while in use. Great Bedroll and Furhide Bedroll also slow Warm to the core decay, but hunger, cold, sickness and interruptions still apply.
guides.image_caption: A Great Bedroll provides sleeping comfort and protection.

guides.title: Foods
paragraphs: Foods differ in satiation, sickness risk and other effects. See each item for stats, recipes and ways to obtain it.
Herbivore increases satiation from foods the game treats as plant-based, not all food. Satiation stops at 100%.

Eating rolls the food's sickness risk. A meal that does not cause sickness may extend Well fed; see Satiation for its trigger and Stamina for its effect. Sickness and Well fed act separately from satiation's ordinary wellbeing contribution.
Honey improves wellbeing and shortens sickness. Bramble Berries and Bursthopper restore stamina; Cranberries restore focus. Riftvine Berries reduce wellbeing. See each item for amounts.
Pleasant Vegetable Soup, Tasty Crab Soup and Survivor's Delight grant temporary warmth. Baby Firelouse also warms you but causes a fire hit.
Recipes list ingredients, outputs, AP and workstation requirements. Check the resulting food's sickness risk: preparation does not always make food safe.
guides.image_caption: Pleasant Vegetable Soup provides food and temporary warmth.

guides.title: Weather
paragraphs: Clear, cloudy and rainy weather can change when a completed turn crosses an hour boundary. Ambient temperature approaches a time-of-day target with small random variation. It is separate from body temperature.
Dry spells increase cloud and rain chances; accumulated rain encourages clearing. The ordered hourly checks are below.
On Easy and Medium, clouds cannot start new rain while fewer than two days have been survived. Hard has no early-game protection. Clouds can still form during the protected period.
Wet clothing can dampen its wearer and other carried clothing. Wetness affects body Temperature; waterproofing, shelter and drying help alongside insulation.

Lesser shelter blocks 80% of rain and stronger shelter blocks 95%. Shelter can cool hot conditions. Nearby active fires warm and dry you. Dungeon-like areas use a separate ambient temperature baseline.
Weather and temperature keep changing while you rest. Check your shelter, clothing and wellbeing trend before sleeping.
guides.image_caption: Protective clothing such as a Traveller's Cloak matters when travelling in wet weather.

guides.title: Action points
paragraphs: Attacking, equipping, crafting and applying remedies each cost AP. Costs can include fractions.
The player normally has 8 AP per turn. Spending the remaining AP ends the turn. The next turn restores AP minus any cost carried over.
Outside combat, some actions can exceed your remaining AP and carry the excess into the next turn. In combat, the required AP must be available.
Unused AP can restore stamina, with swimming and bed-rest exceptions; see Stamina. The clock advances per completed turn, not per AP.
Equipping costs a base 0.4 AP per square of inventory footprint, separate from attacking or using the item.
Fast Draw reduces bow costs, but not orb costs; Blade Master, Master Basher and Force Fighter reduce costs for their weapon types. Brewer reduces alchemy costs.
Completed turns also update satiation, focus, temperature and wellbeing. Rest and sleep change recovery rates but do not pause these meters.

guides.title: Armor points
section_titles: From armor value to armor points
paragraphs: Every equipped item with an armor value adds it to your Total Armor, shown on the equipment screen. Clothing counts as well as armor: shirts, socks, hoods and cloaks often add a fraction of a point. All four hand slots count, so a shield on your inactive weapon set still adds its armor.

Each item adds its armor value multiplied by its current durability divided by its maximum durability, rounded to two decimals. A Steel Chestplate (6 armor, 300 durability) adds 6 when undamaged and 3 at 150 durability. Total Armor is then rounded to one decimal.

When combat begins, Total Armor is rounded down to whole armor points. Fractions are added together before rounding, so a 0.5 shirt, 0.5 pants and 0.1 socks give 1.1 Total Armor and 1 armor point. Each armor point adds one armor layer to one HP cell. A 2.9 total still gives only 2 points.
Each HP cell holds at most three armor layers. You receive at most three points for each HP cell still alive when combat begins; any Total Armor beyond that cap is not used for that fight.

You must place your armor points before combat can proceed. Left-click an HP cell to add a layer and right-click to remove one. Even clears your placement and fills cells row by row from the top left, one layer per cell on each pass. Random clears your placement and puts each point on a random cell. Done finishes placement; any points not yet placed are lost for that fight. Ending your turn is blocked until you press Done.

Equipping armor during combat gives no extra points until the next fight. Unequipping an item with an armor value during combat strips its full undamaged armor value, rounded to the nearest whole number with halves rounding up, from random armored cells. When no hostiles remain, all armor layers are removed until the next fight.
Creatures do not choose placement. Their armor is layered automatically when they appear, row by row from the top left like Even. Their health grids show the result; see Health and armor.

guides.title: Tree health and chopping
paragraphs: Every part of a tree or shrub, from trunk to twig, has its own life value between 0 and 1. The Harvest menu shows it as a freshness label: Very Fresh from about 0.88 life, Fresh from about 0.63, Half Dead from about 0.38, Mostly Dead from about 0.13 and Dead below that. A plant starts at full life, and each new branch starts with the life of the part it grows from.

No. Life never goes back up, but most trees lose almost none. Plants grow only while you are away: when you return to an outdoor area, each plant catches up about one growth step per three hours you were gone, counting at most 240 hours. On each step a part of a Willow, Cypress, Trollgnarl or Elderwort Shrub has a small chance to lose some life. The chance is negligible on low, wet ground and rises the higher the ground sits within the range where the species grows. A trunk at the top of that range loses about a third of its life over a ten-day absence on average, while a lowland tree stays fresh. Low inner branches of tall trees are far more at risk and can die off on high ground. Trees in Withered Mire and Rift-Thorn Mire decay slightly faster, Elderwort Shrubs eight times slower, and Brambles and Rift Vine never lose life this way.

A branch cannot stay much healthier than the part it grows from. On each growth step where a part's parent has lower life, the part's life moves halfway to its parent's. Once a parent falls below 0.33 life, the parts on it stop growing, so a dying trunk drags its whole crown down with it.

Rifts dry out nearby plants of every kind, including Brambles and Rift Vine. When a rift opens, and every in-game hour while it stays open in your area, each plant part within 60 pixels of a small rift or 192 pixels of a large one has a two-in-three chance to lose 0.01 to 0.1 life. That averages about 0.04 life per hour, so a fresh part beside an open rift falls below 0.33 in roughly 18 hours. Plants still catching up on growth are skipped.

A part at 0.33 life or less is dead wood: it shows no leaves and grows no new branches. This point falls inside the Mostly Dead label. Lower life also makes new branches less likely and fades a part toward pale grey. A part at 0.001 life or less becomes fully dead at 0.

Chopping a part costs action points. The cost starts at 24 times the part's size, divided by a dryness factor: the life the part has lost, rounded to the nearest tenth and counted as at least 0.1, times 5. A nearly full-life part costs 48 times its size, a half-dead part 9.6 times and a dead part 4.8 times, so dead wood is ten times cheaper to cut.

On a Willow, Cypress or Trollgnarl the trunk's cost is multiplied by 1.33 plus its size. The menu names a trunk a Branch below size 0.2, a Thick Branch below 0.3 and a Trunk otherwise; other parts are Twigs below 0.2, Branches below 0.4 and Thick Branches above. Every cost is then capped at 32 AP before the species multiplier and the tool are applied.
Willow has no species multiplier, so its hardest fresh cut costs 32 AP before the tool.
Cypress costs 1.2 times as much after the cap, up to 38.4 AP before the tool. It is common in Drowned Fen.
Trollgnarl is the hardest tree to chop: its cost is doubled after the cap, up to 64 AP before the tool. It is common in Withered Mire.

Elderwort Shrub ignores dryness and the trunk multiplier: its stem costs 8 times its size and other parts 4 times theirs. Parts below size 0.33 are Twigs and the rest Branches. It is common in Sunken Ancient Ruins.

Brambles and Rift Vine use only the basic size and dryness cost, and every part is listed as a Twig. Since they never lose life while growing, only rifts dry them out. Rift Vine is common in Rift-Thorn Mire.

The cost is divided by the chopping strength of the tool you pick, rounded to the nearest 0.2 AP, and is never below 0.2 AP. Any carried item with a chopping strength can be picked; with no tool you chop barehanded at strength 1. Felling axes are strongest, while a Serpent Fang doubles the cost. Each successful chop wears down the tool, but bare hands never wear out.

Action points are not whole numbers: a chop takes exactly the cost shown, such as 2.4 AP, and costs are shown to one decimal place. A chop is refused if it costs more than your 8 AP maximum, and a falling part cannot be chopped. Outside combat you may chop with less AP than the cost: your AP drops to 0, your turn ends and the shortfall comes out of your next turn. In combat you must have enough AP. Like any action, chopping tires you; see Stamina.

When the cut lands, the part falls with everything growing from it. With low focus or stamina, or under some effects, a swing can go wrong: the AP is spent, the part stays standing and you lose 2 wellbeing.
guides.image_caption: A Willow; each trunk, branch and twig keeps its own life value.

guides.title: Leeching
paragraphs: Leeching attacks remove armor before the hit point beneath it, like Weak attacks. Each hit point a leeching attack destroys can restore one wounded hit point to the attacker.
Mirkfangs, Giant Mirkfangs, Mirkfang Matriarchs and The Terror attack with Leeching damage.

guides.title: Magic weapons
paragraphs: Orbs are one-handed ranged weapons. They need no ammunition. Each has its own damage type, attack pattern and range: poison, fire, blunt (iron and steel essence), weak (wind) or force (storm).

Every cast drains one of your survival meters: focus for poison orbs, warmth for fire orbs, satiation for essence orbs and stamina for wind and storm. If the meter is lower than the cost, the shortfall is taken from wellbeing instead.

Every cast also uses 1 durability. An orb has 30 durability, so a new one lasts 30 casts and then breaks. Orbs cannot be repaired, and being hit does not wear them. Like other gear, orbs left in ordinary stashes lose durability over time, and orbs found as random treasure are already partly used, with 18 to 29 durability left. Resale value falls with durability.

Orbs can be used at any distance up to their range, including next to an enemy. Fast Draw's AP reduction and free-shot chance apply to bows, not orbs. Master Basher and Force Fighter bonuses apply only to melee weapons, so they do not boost blunt or force orbs.
Staff of The Fire Eater is a two-handed melee fire weapon with no casting cost. Whenever an attack hits more than one cell, it also treats one of your burnt hit points.
Grand Mother at the Survivors' camp sells every orb and the staff. They are not crafted.

guides.title: Survivors' camp
paragraphs: The camp is built the first time you enter a Savage Mirk area, so each world has one. A torchlight message and five white dots point toward it when it appears.
Wilda and three Survivor guards live here. You may trade with Wilda, but you cannot place or build anything within about 26 tiles of the camp. No creatures spawn within 16 tiles of it.

Choose Trust in Wilda's conversation. She asks you to kill The Terror, a Mirkfang Matriarch that stalks the camp's area at night, and bring back the Head of The Terror. The Terror only appears after this request, and only at night. She is never within 16 tiles of the camp's main hut, but can be anywhere else in the camp's 160 x 160-tile area, so search the area at night away from the camp.

Hand the head to Wilda to unlock the ladder to Grand Mother's hut. Grand Mother's first greeting grants one skill point. She sells magic weapons, Summoning Stones and, later in the main quest, Magus' Shard.
Wilda can then be summoned with a Summoning Stone, and the Survivors greet you as a friend.

guides.title: Placing objects
paragraphs: While placing an object, press the Weapon Swap key (Z by default) to flip it horizontally before you confirm.
An object can be placed directly from a nearby container, not only from your inventory.

You cannot place objects within about 26 tiles of the Survivors' camp. Until you bring Viend back to the fort, the same applies within 30 tiles of Fort Solid. Placement also fails on water, slopes, plants, goo and occupied tiles.
Storage Chest is a placeable 7 x 5 container. Items inside lose no durability, stay dry and never go missing, unlike items left in ordinary stashes. Clay and Viend sell it.

guides.title: Strict move
paragraphs: Hold Left Ctrl (the Strict Move key) while clicking to walk to a tile without interacting with whatever is there. Objects are not highlighted while the key is held.
This avoids opening containers, harvesting plants or talking to characters when you only meant to move. Strict Move can be rebound in the key settings.

guides.title: Planting
paragraphs: Seeds are planted the same way you place an object: choose the seed in your inventory, then pick a tile within three tiles of you. Planting costs action points like other placements and uses up one seed. Any grass on the tile is cleared and a seedling appears.

While you hold a seed, the target tile is framed in a color that shows whether the seed can grow there, and nearby tiles get a faint frame: white where the seed would take, red where it would not. Checking these frames is the quickest way to find a spot.

A tile refuses every seed if it is under a solid object, covered in goo or cave spikes, or already holds something rooted, such as a boulder, a log, tall grass, a fern, a lilypad or another planted seed. You cannot plant inside other people's homes or other private areas. Each seed also has its own rules about ground height and ground type.

A Simple Shelter or a Canopy gradually casts deep shade on the tiles beneath it. Deeply shaded tiles refuse seeds, and crops already growing there shrink away, so keep gardens out from under your shelters.
In Fort Solid Shorehold the ground within about six tiles of the fort is kept clear. Until late in the main story, planting there always fails; after that, attempts there still usually fail.

Each seed grows only within its own range of depths and heights, from deep water up to the high plateau; see Terrain for the bands. Watercress Seeds go deepest and are the only seeds for medium and deep water. Cranberry Seeds need grassy shallow water. Trollgnarl Seed Pods only take raised ground.

Apart from Watercress Seeds and Cranberry Seeds, every seed refuses stone, and only Elderberry Seeds accept sand. No seed takes a slope. Mud is fine for every land seed. Each ground kind's page lists the seeds that can grow on it.

Planted seeds grow only while you are away from an area. When you return, the area catches up on the time you missed, up to ten days. Each tile gets a few growth chances per day, so results vary from plant to plant.

Turnip, Cranberry and watercress crops pass through four growth stages and usually need around four to five days away to ripen. Seedlings of Willow, Cypress, Trollgnarl, Elderwort Shrub and Brambles become full-grown plants after about three days away on average, after which they follow the rules in Tree health and chopping.
Crops shrink and eventually disappear on Rift Grass or in deep shade. In Rift-Thorn Mire after the rift has opened, crops stop partway and never fully ripen.
Established crops can seed neighboring tiles that suit them. Cranberries spread readily through suitable shallows, while Turnip and watercress plants spread only now and then.

guides.title: Terrain
paragraphs: Every outdoor tile has a fixed ground height. The game uses it to draw water, soil and slopes, and to decide what grows and what can walk there. Ground heights fall into the bands below, from deep water up to the high plateau. In the water, the game describes how deep you are standing, from "Your feet are slightly submerged" to "You are swimming!".

Every step costs action points depending on the tile you step onto. A diagonal step costs 0.4 AP more, heavy encumbrance raises the cost, and no single step costs more than 8 AP. Obstacles, water and the ground underneath combine: wading over sand or mud costs more than wading over soil.

Water levels never change. Heights are set when an area is generated and are not touched by rain, time or weather afterwards, so a dry tile stays dry and a pool never spreads or drains. Rain only adds splash ripples to water and wets your clothes. The dark stains some tiles show are blood or acid, not wet ground.

Each kind of ground has its own page covering where it appears, which creatures spawn and walk there, which seeds take, and whether you can build on it. The table summarizes them. The creature table column says which spawn table picks creatures that appear on that ground; see Areas.

A Boulder or a water rock costs 2.5 AP to clamber over. A Mossy Log, ruin rubble or debris costs 1.8 AP. Tall Grass and Fern patches add up to about half as much again as they grow, and bramble thickets and Rift Vine growth cost far more. Water rocks only appear in medium or deep water and give dry footing there. None of these tiles can be built on or planted.
A lit Campfire slowly scorches the ground beneath it into black ash. Ash walks like bare soil at 0.8 AP a step.

Strider removes 8% of the extra cost of obstacles and thick growth per rank, Amphibian removes 8% of the extra cost of water per rank, and Firm Grip makes slopes cheaper with each rank. Balance and Jumper help with jumping across gaps rather than walking.

Every land creature can wade into the shallows, but only some go deeper, as the table shows. The Mudfin and the Razorfin cannot enter the shore shallows. Any creature can stand on a water rock, a log or the dock. Spawning ignores these limits, so a Mudfin can appear stuck in the shore shallows until it is attacked.

guides.title: Soil
paragraphs: Bare soil is the ground under everything else outdoors. Its color shows its height: dark soil at the waterline, ordinary brown on low ground, and lighter soil on the plateaus. Grass, mud, sand and stone are laid on top of it. See Terrain for the height bands.
Soil is the base of every outdoor area except Vast Waters, which is all open water. Where nothing else covers it, it shows as bare earth.

Walking onto soil costs 0.8 AP, the cheapest outdoor step. You can build and place objects on it, as long as nothing else stands, grows or lies on the tile. A lit Campfire slowly scorches the soil beneath it to ash, which walks the same.
Soil takes every land seed. Which ones depends on its height, as listed below. Cranberry Seeds and Watercress Seeds need water instead.

Creatures appearing on soil come from the area's land table, which depends on the area, the time of day and the main story; see each area page. Every walking creature can cross it. Only the water creatures stay off it: the Mudfin, the Razorfin and the Mire Serpent. Flying creatures go anywhere.

guides.title: Grassy ground
paragraphs: Most dry ground and the shore shallows are covered in grass. Short grass is a few blades over soil. Thick grass grows until it covers the ground. Moss grows on stone and inside caves and ruins. Rift Grass replaces ordinary grass around the rift.

Grass grows anywhere from the shore shallows upward, in every outdoor area except Vast Waters. It stays short and thin in the Withered Mire, on mud, and in deep shade. Moss covers about a third of the stony patches in every area. Rift Grass spreads through the Rift-Thorn Mire until the rift is dealt with.

Short grass, moss and Rift Grass cost 0.8 AP a step, like bare soil. Thick grass costs 1.0 AP, and thick grass growing through shallow water 1.4 AP. Tall Grass and Fern patches are separate plants that slow you further. You can build and place objects on it, as long as nothing else stands, grows or lies on the tile.

Grass does not change which land seeds take. They follow the soil height underneath, and planting clears the grass. Thick grass or moss growing through shallow water is what Cranberry Seeds need. Crops on Rift Grass shrink away instead of growing, and moss on dry stone still counts as stone, which refuses seeds.

Creatures on grassy ground come from the area's land table; see each area page. In the Rift-Thorn Mire, Rift Grass tiles use the rift table like every other tile there. Every walking creature can cross it. Only the water creatures stay off it: the Mudfin, the Razorfin and the Mire Serpent. Flying creatures go anywhere.

guides.title: Sand
paragraphs: Pale sand covers beaches and scattered sandy patches. It slopes gently from dry ground into the water.

Any side of a land area that faces the edge of the world, a Vast Waters area or a Broken Fen becomes a sandy beach about thirty tiles deep, dropping into deep water. A Broken Fen has beaches on all four sides. Every land area also gets a few inland sandy patches: two to six per area, or 24 in the Withered Mire.

Sand is heavy going at 1.2 AP a step. Wading over a sandy bottom also costs more than over soil: 1.4 AP in shallow water, 2.0 AP in medium water and 5 AP in deep water. You can build and place objects on it, as long as nothing else stands, grows or lies on the tile.
Elderberry Seeds are the only land seed that takes on dry sand, from the upper half of the waterline up. Under water, Watercress Seeds ignore the bottom and grow on sand at their usual depth.

Dry sand has its own spawn table in every area except the Rift-Thorn Mire, day and night alike. The Boulder Crab is by far the most common creature on it, and bird nests are often built on sand. Every walking creature can cross it. Only the water creatures stay off it: the Mudfin, the Razorfin and the Mire Serpent. Flying creatures go anywhere.

guides.title: Mud
paragraphs: Dark, wet mud lies in winding streaks across low ground. It is dry ground, not water.

Every land area has 16 to 24 winding mud streaks, laid between the waterline and the first plateau. A Broken Fen has only about a third as many. Calmia Root plants grow only on mud, so mud is where to look for them.
Mud costs 1.2 AP a step, the same as sand. You can build and place objects on it, as long as nothing else stands, grows or lies on the tile.
Mud takes every land seed at the right height, just like soil. Grass on mud never grows thick, so muddy shallows are no good for Cranberry Seeds.

Creatures on mud come from the area's land table; see each area page. Every walking creature can cross it. Only the water creatures stay off it: the Mudfin, the Razorfin and the Mire Serpent. Flying creatures go anywhere.

guides.title: Stone ground
paragraphs: Grey rock breaks through the soil in stony patches. Some patches are overgrown with moss. Old ruins add squares of paving and broken paths.

Every land area has about 48 stony patches, or 80 in the Withered Mire and about 14 in a Broken Fen. Stony patches can reach into shallow and medium water. Each area also has 4 to 8 paved ruin squares, while the Sunken Ancient Ruins have 32 to 48 large ones plus paved paths.
Stone and paving cost 0.8 AP a step, like soil. You can build and place objects on it, as long as nothing else stands, grows or lies on the tile.

Dry stone refuses every land seed, with or without moss, and so does paving. In the water, mossy stone in the shallows suits Cranberry Seeds, and Watercress Seeds grow on any bottom at their usual depth.

Creatures on stone come from the area's land table; see each area page. Every walking creature can cross it. Only the water creatures stay off it: the Mudfin, the Razorfin and the Mire Serpent. Flying creatures go anywhere.

rows: About 48 patches, 32 to 48 large ruin squares and paved paths

guides.title: Goo
paragraphs: Glistening violet goo seeps from the rift and pools over the ground. Stepping in it gives the message that your feet are entirely submerged, but it is never deep enough to swim in.
Goo is found only in the Rift-Thorn Mire, which has 48 to 56 spreading pools, and in the rift depths below it.
Goo costs 1.2 AP a step outdoors and 1.0 AP in the rift depths. You cannot build, place objects or plant on it.
No seed takes on goo.
Every creature in the Rift-Thorn Mire, on goo or anywhere else, comes from the rift table; see Rift-Thorn Mire. Any creature can wade into goo.

guides.title: Dock planks
paragraphs: The wooden dock where your boat arrives at Fort Solid Shorehold. The planks are built over deep water.
Only at Fort Solid Shorehold, beside the fort.
The dock costs 0.8 AP a step and never adds a water penalty, even though water lies beneath. You cannot build or plant on it, because the game treats it as water.

The dock counts as dry footing, so any creature can walk onto it, including the walkers that cannot enter deep water. Creatures that appear on the dock come from the water table, because there is water under the planks.

tables.caption: The water table, used day and night in every area except Rift-Thorn Mire. Fort Solid Shorehold never uses tougher forms.

guides.title: Slopes
paragraphs: Slopes are the steep edges of raised ground, drawn as banks and cliffs. A slope rings the edge of each first plateau and each high plateau above it.
Every land area has hills and plateaus. The Withered Mire has by far the most, with many raised hills and a base higher than any other area. Vast Waters has none.
Climbing a slope costs 5 AP a step. Each rank of Firm Grip makes it cheaper. You cannot build or plant on a slope. The flat plateau top beyond the slope walks like soil at 0.8 AP.
No seed takes on a slope. Trollgnarl Seed Pods do well on the plateau tops.

Creatures appearing on a slope come from the area's land table. Creatures can climb slopes but never choose one as a place to wander to, so they mostly stay on level ground. Bird nests are often built on slopes. Every walking creature can cross it. Only the water creatures stay off it: the Mudfin, the Razorfin and the Mire Serpent. Flying creatures go anywhere.

guides.title: Shallow water
paragraphs: Shallow water lies just below the waterline. The game says your feet are submerged. It comes in two bands. In the shore shallows, nearest the bank, grass still grows through the water. The open shallows, a little deeper, are bare water over dark soil.

Every land area has shallow water along its pools and shores and in scattered puddles: about 40 puddles in most areas, 800 in the Drowned Fen, 12 in the Withered Mire and 5 in a Broken Fen. Beaches and lakes have a band of it around their edges.
Water levels never change, so shallow water stays shallow. You can attack and jump as usual, and your pack stays dry.

Wading costs 1.2 AP a step over soil or stone, and 1.4 AP over sand, mud or thick grass. Each rank of Amphibian takes 8% off the water's share. You cannot build or place anything in shallow water, not even a Raft Base.

Shallow water takes four seeds. Cranberry Seeds need thick grass or moss growing through the water. Willow Seeds take the shore shallows, Cypress Seed Pods take both bands, and Watercress Seeds take all but the top edge of the open shallows.

Creatures that appear in shallow water come from the water table. Every land creature can wade into shallow water. Mudfin and Razorfin can swim in the open shallows but not the shore shallows. The Mire Serpent stays in medium and deep water.

guides.title: Medium water
paragraphs: Medium water lies between the shallows and deep water and is greener and denser than the shallows. The game says your legs are submerged.

Ponds and lakes in every land area have a band of medium water. There is much more of it in the Drowned Fen and the Broken Fen. Water rocks only appear in medium or deep water, and lilypads float on medium water and the upper part of deep water.
Water levels never change. In medium water your pack stays dry, but jumps take a penalty of 3.

Wading costs 1.6 AP a step over soil or stone and 2.0 AP over sand or mud. Amphibian reduces the water's share. A water rock costs 2.5 AP but keeps you out of the water. The only thing you can place here is a Raft Base, and not on a water rock. A raft moves at 1.8 AP a step.
Watercress Seeds take all medium water. Cypress Seed Pods take its upper half.

Creatures that appear here come from the water table. Whenever you end a move here outside Fort Solid Shorehold, there is a 2% chance a Mire Serpent bursts out of the water beside you. Small walkers such as the Giant Slug, the Viper, the Mirk Runner and the Boulder Crab cannot enter medium water. Larger walkers such as the Swamp Troll, the Toadkin and the Scaalmyr can. Swimmers and the Mire Serpent move freely here.

tables.caption: The water table, used day and night in every area except Rift-Thorn Mire. Fort Solid Shorehold never uses tougher forms.

guides.title: Deep water
paragraphs: Deep water is the lowest band, teal and opaque. At its edge you stand waist-deep. Further in the water reaches your chest, then your shoulders, and in the deepest water you swim.

Lakes in every land area have deep middles, and every beach drops into deep water. A Broken Fen is mostly deep water between islands. The fort's dock stands over deep water. A Vast Waters area is entirely deep water, all of it at swimming depth.

Water levels never change. In deep water your pack gets wet. From chest depth you cannot attack ("The water is too deep!") and combat ends. From shoulder depth you cannot jump, and before that jumps take a penalty of 7.

Swimming costs 0.15 stamina a turn, more when overburdened, so a full stamina bar lasts about six or seven turns. When it runs out you start drowning, and after four turns you die. Standing on a raft or a water rock stops it.

Wading or swimming costs 3.4 AP a step over soil or stone and 5 AP over sand or mud. The only thing you can place here is a Raft Base, not on a water rock. A raft moves at 1.8 AP a step and never swims or drowns, so it is the safe way across.
Watercress Seeds take the top of deep water, down to about waist depth. Nothing else grows here.

Creatures that appear here come from the water table. Ending a move here outside the fort's area has a 2% chance of a Mire Serpent surging up beside you. Only flyers, swimmers and the Mire Serpent can enter deep water. Every walker stops at its edge, which makes it a refuge from them.

tables.caption: The water table, used day and night in every area except Rift-Thorn Mire. Fort Solid Shorehold never uses tougher forms.

guides.title: Interior floors
paragraphs: Caves, ruin buildings, cellars, the rift depths and people's homes have their own floors. Cave floors are bare rock. Ruin and cellar floors are old stone slabs with moss. The rift depths have dark, alien ground with goo and pits.

Cave mouths are scattered through every land area. In the Sunken Ancient Ruins most of them lead to cellars and ruined buildings instead. The rift depths lie under the Rift-Thorn Mire opposite the fort. Homes belong to people such as Ranger Bhato and Gurb-Gurb.
Interior floors cost 0.8 AP a step. Rubble costs 2.5 AP, husks in the deepest rift chamber 1.6 AP and cave spikes 5 AP. You can build on open floor except in other people's homes.
Cave and ruin floors count as stone, so seeds refuse them. Planting on rift-depth floors has not been tested.

Caves and ruin interiors do not spawn creatures turn by turn. Each time you return after at least a day, a cave may restock with up to four creatures, about one for every two days away, and grows new Vile Bulb mushrooms. Ruin buildings and cellars restock the same way from a different list. The two outer rift chambers spawn every turn, up to 8 or 12 creatures. Homes never spawn creatures.

guides.title: Areas
paragraphs: The world map is a five-by-five grid of areas. The game calls each one an area, as in "Entering new area" and "Map of area", and names it by its kind, such as Common Bog or Drowned Fen. There are nine kinds. The kind shapes the land, which trees and plants grow, which creatures roam and what landmarks you can find. Caves, ruin buildings, cellars and homes are separate interiors entered from an area.

Every world follows the same recipe. After the fixed kinds are placed, the leftover cells are split roughly evenly between Common Bog, Withered Mire and Drowned Fen, so a world can lack a Withered Mire entirely.

Any side of a land area that faces the edge of the world, a Vast Waters area or a Broken Fen becomes a sandy beach about thirty tiles deep that drops into deep water. A Broken Fen has beaches on all four sides. See Terrain for the ground itself.

Each time you end a turn of eight minutes, the area may add one creature, or a small group, at a random spot out of your sight and outside private ground. Nothing more appears once 24 creatures are about. In real-time combat, 95% of turns add nothing. The ground at the chosen spot picks the table: every tile in the Rift-Thorn Mire uses its rift table; elsewhere water tiles use the water table, dry sand the sand table, and other ground the area's land table. Each area page lists its land table.
The water and sand tables are the same in every area except the Rift-Thorn Mire, and they do not change with the time of day or the story.

Outside Fort Solid Shorehold, some creatures can appear as a tougher form. In the Savage Mirk they always do. A Giant Mirkfang, including one upgraded from a Mirkfang, is a Mirkfang Matriarch 4% of the time.

The land tables change as the main story moves on. From the journal entry "Bring the rune back", Sceetlers join them. From "Escort Viend", Scaalmyr Grunts and Mutated Unwanted join too, and a Grunt brings a Sceetler 52.5% of the time. After "Scaal defeated", 95% of Scaalmyr spawns are cancelled and re-rolled elsewhere. Scaalmyr then make up under 1% of land spawns: 0.90% by day and 0.72% at night, or 0.63% and 0.54% in the Withered Mire. The Rift-Thorn Mire falls to about a 46% chance of any spawn each turn.

Whenever you end a move, on foot or by raft, in medium or deep water anywhere but Fort Solid Shorehold, there is a 2% chance a Mire Serpent surges out beside you. It never appears any other way. At night, each turn has a 50% chance of releasing one to four Firefly lights while fewer than five are about.

Each new tree's kind is drawn from the area's mix before a spot is chosen. A kind that cannot grow at the chosen spot simply fails, so kinds with a narrow height range, such as Trollgnarl and Cypress, end up rarer than the table suggests.

Each area is stocked with wild plants, bird nests and skeletons when it is first made. A skeleton is sometimes a treasure chest instead. A chest is a common chest 88.2% of the time, a richer chest 9.8% and a treasure chest 2%. They have value budgets of roughly 3 to 20, 5 to 40 and 10 to 50, filled with a few valuable items rather than many cheap ones.

A bird nest gives 1 to 7 Feathers (2.5 on average), an Egg or more 40% of the time, and a small trinket 5% of the time. Ground litter gives a Rock, Twigs or both, plus independent chances of extra finds.

Weather, the time of day and the outdoor temperature are shared by the whole world. When you return to an area it catches up on up to ten days. Plants grow, new Calmia Root plants appear on mud (two per day away, except in the Rift-Thorn Mire), nests and rubble refill, and after a day or more felled trees are gradually replaced toward about 120.

guides.title: Fort Solid Shorehold
section_titles: Creatures in water and on sand
paragraphs: Every game begins here. The area sits on the left or right edge of the world map, so at least one side is beach. Its neighbors are Common Bog areas, except that one of them can be Vast Waters.

Ordinary mixed swamp with a flattened, open middle. The fort stands in a fenced clearing beside the wooden dock where your boat arrives. Elsewhere lies an abandoned camp next to a rift, with a Campfire and a few supplies left in containers.
Captain Eir and the fort's Soldier garrison live here, and the fort building leads inside.

This is the safest area. Creatures here never appear as their tougher forms, and the Mire Serpent never ambushes from the water. Its land table does not change with the story, so no Scaalmyr spawn here. Creatures that appear on land here are drawn from the table below. Night runs from dusk to dawn. Water and sand tiles use the shared tables underneath.
The shared water and sand tables apply, without tougher forms.
The usual mix, mostly Willow and Brambles.
Skeletons here are the least likely of any area to be treasure chests, and none lie close to the fort.

Early in the story you cannot build within about thirty tiles of the fort, and the ground around it counts as private. At night the soldiers walk you back inside if you linger nearby, until later in the story. Seeds cannot take within about six tiles of the fort. At one point in the main story Viend will not let you leave the area.

section_titles: Creatures in water and on sand
paragraphs: Withered Mire areas fill some of the map's leftover cells, so a world can have several or none.

Sandy and stony patches are common, and scattered ruin walls and rubble are much more common than elsewhere, where most of them are boulders instead.

The Firelouse and Raving Unwanted are common here day and night. Creatures that appear on land here are drawn from the table below. Night runs from dusk to dawn. Water and sand tiles use the shared tables underneath.
The shared water and sand tables apply. With so much sand, Boulder Crabs are common.
Grass stays short and thin. Trollgnarl makes up a third of new trees, and trees here die off faster than in most areas.
Bird nests are twice as plentiful, on the slopes and sand. The stunted grass leaves few tiles for Cranberry Seeds, but the high, dry ground suits turnips, brambles and trollgnarls.

Cypress is three times as common as usual, about one new tree in seven.
Cranberry patches are abundant, and there are twice the usual Calmia Root plants. The shallows suit Cypress Seed Pods, Willow Seeds, Cranberry Seeds and Watercress Seeds.

guides.title: Broken Fen
section_titles: Creatures in water and on sand
paragraphs: Each world has two or three Broken Fens. Neighboring areas treat a Broken Fen like open sea, so their shared edges become beaches.

An archipelago: beaches on all four sides drop into deep water, leaving sandy islands and shallows in between. Only about a third of the usual rocks, logs, trees, nests and plants appear, so it looks sparse and open. The world map draws it as water.

Most of the area is water or sand, so the water and sand tables supply most creatures. On the few patches of firmer land, the table is the same as in the Common Bog. Creatures that appear on land here are drawn from the table below. Night runs from dusk to dawn. Water and sand tiles use the shared tables underneath.
Mudfin and Boulder Crabs are the usual company. Ending a move in medium or deep water risks a Mire Serpent.
The usual mix, but only 48 to 72 trees to start with. Felled or missing trees regrow toward the usual number over later visits.
Broken Fens hold the most loot of any area: more skeletons than usual, and a quarter of them are treasure chests.
Ihar's shipwreck is placed on a shoreline of the first Broken Fen you enter. If it does not fit there, the game tries again in the next Broken Fen you enter.

paragraphs: Each world has two or three Savage Mirk areas.
The terrain looks like an ordinary bog, but Calmia Root plants are more plentiful here than anywhere else.

The most dangerous kind of area: every creature with a tougher form always appears as it. The Viper is always a Red Fang, the Dreadfly a Deathfly, the Mirk Runner a Mirk Mauler and the Mirkfang a Giant Mirkfang. 4% of Giant Mirkfang are a Mirkfang Matriarch. Mudfin always come as Razorfin and Boulder Crabs as Titanspine Crabs.

Skeletons are more numerous than usual, and one in ten is a treasure chest.

The Survivors' camp is built in the first Savage Mirk you enter, with torchlight pointing the way. Wilda, the Survivor group and Grand Mother live there. Building close to the camp is not allowed. Rifts near the camp go dead, and vines, skeletons and chests right beside it are cleared.

guides.title: Rift-Thorn Mire
paragraphs: Each world has two or three Rift-Thorn Mires. One always sits directly opposite Fort Solid Shorehold on the world map and holds the way down into the rift depths.
The rift has corrupted the land. Pools of goo spread across the ground and Rift Grass replaces ordinary grass. Rifts dot the area, and areas near the rift's own area also get some.

Rift creatures rule here on every kind of ground, even in the water, from the start of the game. No animals, Mudfin or Boulder Crabs spawn here, but a Mire Serpent can still surge out of medium or deep water.
Far fewer trees, and about a quarter are Rift Vine. Trees die off faster here than anywhere else.

While the rift is active, no lilypads, watercress, bird nests, Calmia Root plants, wild turnips or cranberries are placed, and Calmia Root does not come back on later visits. Crops on Rift Grass wither and goo cannot be planted, so this is a poor place for a garden.
After "Scaal defeated", 95% of rift creature spawns are cancelled, leaving about a 46% chance of any spawn each turn. Rift Grass and Rift Vine stop growing, and crops still cannot fully ripen.

guides.title: Vast Waters
paragraphs: Each world has between two and six Vast Waters areas, and one can sit beside Fort Solid Shorehold. Land areas next to one get a beach along the shared edge.
Open sea. The whole area is deep water at swimming depth, with no ground, trees, plants, nests or skeletons. The world map draws it as water.
You can travel in from any neighboring edge, swimming or on a raft.

Swimming costs 0.15 stamina a turn, more when overburdened, so a full bar lasts about six or seven turns. When stamina runs out you start drowning, and four turns later you die. You cannot attack while swimming. A raft never swims or drowns and moves at 1.8 AP a step, so it is the safe way across.
Every tile is water, so every creature comes from the water table. Normal tougher-form odds apply. Ending a move here, swimming or rafting, has a 2% chance of a Mire Serpent.

Plant Turnip Seeds on dry land: low ground a little back from the waterline and both plateaus, though not the very highest hilltops. Soil, grass and mud all take them. Stone, sand, slopes and tiles under solid objects refuse them. See Planting for the height bands.

Cranberry Seeds only take in shallow water that has thick grass or moss growing through it, which in practice means the shore shallows. Bare open shallows, deeper water, muddy shallows (grass on mud never grows thick enough), slopes and tiles under solid objects refuse them.
Thick grass is scarcer in Withered Mire, and in Rift-Thorn Mire once the rift has opened, so good cranberry tiles are harder to find there.

Plant Elderberry Seeds anywhere from the upper half of the waterline up to the top of the high plateau. Unlike most seeds they accept sand. Stone, slopes and tiles under solid objects refuse them. They grow into an Elderwort Shrub.

Plant Watercress Seeds in all but the top edge of the open shallows, in any medium water, and in deep water down to waist depth. The bottom does not matter, only the depth. The shore shallows and dry land are too high, and deep water where you would swim is too deep.
Plant Bramble Seeds on the upper half of low ground and on both plateaus. Stone, sand, slopes and tiles under solid objects refuse them.
Plant Willow Seeds in the shore shallows, the waterline, low ground and the first plateau, but not the high plateau. Stone, sand, slopes and tiles under solid objects refuse them.
Plant Cypress Seed Pods in the upper half of medium water, both shallow bands, the waterline and low ground. Both plateaus are too high. Stone, sand, slopes and tiles under solid objects refuse them.
Trollgnarl Seed Pods only take on the upper half of the first plateau and on the high plateau, away from the slopes at their edges. Stone, sand and tiles under solid objects refuse them.

factions.title: Survivor camp faction
factions.summary: Wilda, Grand Mother and the Survivors share this faction. Like friendly NPCs, they skip the player and each other during normal target acquisition, but can retaliate when attacked.

factions.title: Mirkfang faction
factions.summary: Mirkfangs, Giant Mirkfangs, Mirkfang Matriarchs and The Terror share a faction and normally avoid targeting one another.

paragraphs: Beings normally avoid targeting their own faction. Nightmare, Raving Unwanted and Clay's boss form are exceptions: they can target each other, but never themselves. Late in the story, Captain Eir and Magus Clay also treat each other as enemies.
Friendly NPCs and the Survivor camp faction also avoid targeting the player, who belongs to a separate faction.
An eligible target must still pass distance, detection, reachability and sometimes line-of-sight checks. Aggression chance and current targets also matter.

Creatures without a current target often ignore other creatures: wildlife, Giant Slugs, Toadkin, the Nightmare faction, trolls and Mirkfangs pass over a non-player target 60% of the time. Hostile creatures may also give up a chase once you are more than one and a half times their targeting distance away.
Taking damage can make a being retaliate without the usual faction check. Friendly NPCs and faction-mates can therefore fight back.
